summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). If a report is marked **indicated**, the full § 26-14-7.1 hearing (counsel, witnesses, cross-examination, subpoenas, an impartial hearing officer) is available only to a person connected with a facility, agency, or home that cares for and controls children; everyone else, including a parent investigated at home, receives the DHR administrative record review, which DHR describes as "provided for those persons not entitled to a hearing" and for which the DHR review page states no deadline (dhr.alabama.gov/child-protective-services/child-abuse-neglect-administrative-reviews).

key_cases.case_name: Randolph County Department of Human Resources v. A.H.
key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the juvenile court's judgment denying DHR's dependency petition and returning the child to his parents, holding that DHR's abandonment theory was unpreserved and that it had not challenged the finding that the mother could provide the necessary care.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what happens when a filed dependency petition is not supported by evidence of dependency.
key_cases.quote: This court cannot consider an issue raised for the first time on appeal

key_cases.case_name: N.G. v. Blount County Department of Human Resources
key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency findings based on the mother's medication abuse and domestic violence and held that an indigent parent has no constitutional right to appointed counsel in a dependency proceeding, although Ala. Code 12-15-308(c) obliges the juvenile court to advise a parent of the right to counsel at the 72-hour shelter-care hearing and to investigate indigency.
key_cases.relevance: It applies the clear-and-convincing standard to the dependency adjudication that follows the petition.
key_cases.quote: an indigent parent does not have a constitutional right to the appointment of an attorney in a dependency proceeding

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court restated the two-prong termination test - statutory grounds first, then consideration and rejection of all viable alternatives - and held that when a nonparent, including the State, is the petitioner it must additionally prove the child's dependency as a threshold matter.
key_cases.relevance: Beasley fixes what the State must be prepared to prove when it files a dependency or termination petition: dependency as a threshold, plus statutory grounds.
key_cases.quote: if a nonparent, including the State, is the petitioner, then such a petitioner must meet the further threshold proof of dependency

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the parents' Rule 60(b) motions to set aside a dependency judgment, holding that any failure to appoint counsel for the indigent mother implicated only a statutory right under Ala. Code 12-15-305(b) and not constitutional due process, so the judgment was not void and could be challenged only by appeal.
key_cases.relevance: A parent contesting a dependency petition has a statutory, not constitutional, claim to appointed counsel, and the remedy for its denial is a timely appeal rather than a collateral attack.
key_cases.quote: if the juvenile court erred by not appointing counsel for the mother, as an indigent parent, that error affected only a statutory right and not a constitutional due-process right
